summary: David Walden notes that the new message-id bits from RFC 533 give lost message detection almost for free, since the four extra bits can act like the sequence number Hathaway proposed in RFC 512, and describes three ways hosts can use them. It builds on RFC 512 and RFC 516.

eli5.summary: If each message carries a small counter, the receiver can see when one is missing, so the number labels already cover this.

questions: how to detect lost messages with message-id
what is a 16 element sequence number in the imp
subtitle: The extra message-id bits from RFC 533 can serve as a sequence number for spotting lost messages.

tldr.problem: Hosts want a way to detect lost messages, as proposed in RFC 512 and RFC 516.
tldr.mechanism: The four extra message-id bits can be treated as a 16 element sequence number per connection, with element 0 meaning that sequence numbers are not in use.
tldr.outcome: The note describes three ways hosts can use the field, and says that with synchronized ids very reliable retransmission schemes are readily available.

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 534 as Unknown and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 533.

sections.title: Message-ID as a Sequence Number
sections.content:
As an aside to RFC 533, if sending Hosts uniquely identify messages on a link with the extra four bits and receiving Hosts look at them, a lost message detection system like those in RFC 512 and RFC 516 drops right out.

The four bits can be treated as Hathaway's SCB of RFC 512, giving a 16 element sequence number per connection. That is enough because the IMPs never allow more than four outstanding messages at one time between a given pair of Hosts. The 0 element can tell the receiver that sequence numbers are not being used.
sections.eli5: Number your letters 1, 2, 3 and so on. If the receiver sees 3 after 1, it knows number 2 is missing.

sections.title: Three Modes of Use
sections.content:
The note lists three ways to use the message-id under the Host/Host protocol.

  • The sender always sets the extra four bits to 0 and sends only one message over a link at a time. This is slow, but allows orderly retransmission without help from the receiver.
  • The receiver gives no help. Whether the sender uses the bits or not, it cannot retransmit in an orderly way, though uniquely identified messages let it say which one was lost.
  • The sender has several messages outstanding (RFNMs not yet received) and the receiver helps. If the ids are synchronized, for example sequential, the receiver can reliably detect lost messages.
sections.eli5: You can send one letter and wait, send many with no help, or send many while a friend counts them for you.

sections.title: Retransmission Schemes
sections.content:
The author admits the approach may seem insufficient to some, but says that with synchronized unique message-ids very reliable retransmission schemes are readily available.

Two examples are given. The sender can retransmit the appropriate messages after an incomplete transmission, and the receiver can use the ids to sort retransmitted messages into order. Or the receiver can discard all messages that arrive out of order, and the sender can back up and resend the failed message and everything after it.
sections.eli5: Either the receiver puts late letters back in order, or it throws out mixed-up ones and the sender starts again from the missing one.
